claims.claim_text: Dragos counted 1,140 industrial ransomware incidents in Q2 2026 (1,020 in Q1); 176 concerned construction, reported by Dragos as a manufacturing subsector within the 747 manufacturing claims, with Europe at 316 and North America at 514.
claims.exact_locator: Key Findings; Ransomware by Sector - Manufacturing; Ransomware by Region
alternative_hypotheses: Counts reflect leak-site visibility rather than true attack frequency
claims.contrary_evidence: Dragos notes counts are alleged claims and include bulk disclosures
claims.sector_relevance: Places construction among the most frequently claimed industrial victim groups in the reporting period
claims.limitations: Leak-site claims only; sector assignment method not stated; not a sector attack rate

claims.claim_text: Dragos reports that suppliers of building materials, construction services and equipment were repeatedly targeted, linking this to reliance on ERP systems, distributed locations and tight project timelines.
claims.exact_locator: Ransomware by Sector - Manufacturing subsection
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Identifies materials and equipment suppliers as a concentration point for contractor supply
claims.limitations: Qualitative statement; no supplier-level counts

claims.claim_text: Black Kite recorded 7,551 publicly disclosed ransomware victims between April 2025 and March 2026 (up 24.9%); construction ranked third with 541 victims, while Germany rose 48% to 281 and Italy 96% to 188 across all sectors.
claims.exact_locator: Report landing page: headline totals, industry ranking, regional growth
alternative_hypotheses: Growth may reflect group posting behaviour
claims.contrary_evidence: Black Kite states true attack volume is almost certainly higher than leak sites show
claims.sector_relevance: Confirms construction prominence over a 12-month window and rising European victim counts
claims.limitations: Publicly disclosed victims only; construction share not stated; country figures are cross-sector

claims.claim_text: QBE and Control Risks report that ransomware incidents in construction averaged 24 days of downtime in 2025, that inadequate IT/OT segmentation contributed to 81% of OT incident cases in 2025 (Dragos data), and that ransomware groups affected 526 construction organisations in 2025 (Dragos data).
claims.exact_locator: Report page statistics list; press release p.2, p.11 references
claims.contrary_evidence: Methodology for the downtime average is not disclosed
claims.sector_relevance: Quantifies the operational interruption that drives programme delay and cost
claims.limitations: Downtime basis undisclosed; OT figure is cross-industrial, not construction-only

claims.claim_text: In a 2023 survey cited by QBE, 77% of respondents said they could tolerate no more than five days without project documentation before severe operational impact.
claims.exact_locator: Report page: downtime and ransomware statistics
claims.contrary_evidence: Survey population and sample not disclosed on the page
claims.sector_relevance: Indicates low tolerance for loss of shared project-information platforms
claims.limitations: Historical survey (2023) relayed by a 2026 report; population unknown

claims.claim_text: ENISA analysed 4,875 incidents from July 2024 to June 2025: phishing accounted for about 60% of observed initial access and vulnerability exploitation for 21.3%; public administration was the most targeted sector at 38%; OT threats were 18.2% and supply-chain threats 10.6% of threat categories.
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: EU baseline showing identity and edge exploitation as the dominant entry routes, relevant to contractors and public owners
claims.limitations: Observation period ends June 2025; construction not separately analysed

claims.claim_text: The UK NCSC handled 429 incidents in the year to August 2025, of which 204 were nationally significant (89 in the prior year) and 18 highly significant.
claims.exact_locator: Opening paragraphs of release
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: UK national incident baseline for the period preceding the reporting window
claims.limitations: No sector breakdown; change partly reflects NCSC categorisation

claims.claim_text: The November 2025 update to the joint Akira advisory reports about USD 244.17 million in proceeds as of late September 2025, initial access through VPNs without MFA, SonicWall and Cisco vulnerabilities and unpatched Veeam backup servers, and data exfiltration in just over two hours in some incidents; construction is not among the sectors listed.
claims.exact_locator: Update note p.3; Initial Access p.6; Exfiltration and Impact p.9
claims.contrary_evidence: Construction not named as a target sector
claims.sector_relevance: Shows the access routes and speed relevant to contractors running remote-access and backup estates
claims.limitations: Group-specific; proceeds are criminal revenue, not victim loss

claims.claim_text: The Australian Federal Police reported AUD 152.6 million stolen through business email compromise in 2024 (up 66% from AUD 91.6 million), BEC at 13% of business cybercrime reports, and warned that criminals target construction firms because of high-value, frequent transactions, using spoofed or compromised supplier email to replace bank details on invoices.
claims.exact_locator: Release body: figures, modus operandi and case studies
claims.contrary_evidence: Loss figure is economy-wide, not construction-specific
claims.sector_relevance: Payment-chain fraud directly affects contractor and subcontractor liquidity and bank payment flows
claims.limitations: Australian data; the loss total covers all sectors

claims.claim_text: The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security judged it very likely that Iran would use its cyber programme in response to the US/Israel strikes of February 2026 and noted that Iranian state-sponsored actors opportunistically target poorly secured infrastructure networks and internet-connected devices, naming water and energy.
claims.exact_locator: Key judgements; targeting section
claims.contrary_evidence: Construction and building systems not named
claims.sector_relevance: Raises the geopolitical threat to internet-exposed OT used by public-works operators and connected sites
claims.limitations: Canadian perspective; estimative language, not observation

claims.claim_text: On 13 October 2026 Femern A/S stated that its main contractor Femern Link Contractors (FLC) had informed it of a cyber incident and that it had no further information.
claims.exact_locator: News item body, Jens Villemoes quotes
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Confirms an in-period incident at a major European cross-border infrastructure construction programme
claims.limitations: No scope, cause, duration or cost disclosed

claims.claim_text: Danish and German media reported, without owner confirmation, that problems began overnight into Monday 12 October 2026, that large parts of FLC's network were shut down, that staff were told not to use computers, Wi-Fi or contractor email, that digital access control and time registration were unavailable and that several vessels stopped; the project had already been reported in May 2026 as about two years delayed for non-cyber reasons.
claims.exact_locator: S-002 body; S-003 schedule section; S-004 lead paragraphs
alternative_hypotheses: Effects may be precautionary isolation rather than attacker action
claims.contrary_evidence: Owner statement gives no operational detail
claims.sector_relevance: Illustrates how contractor IT disruption can reach marine and site operations
claims.limitations: Reported effects unconfirmed; any schedule or cost effect unknown; pre-existing delay must not be attributed to the incident

claims.claim_text: Kensington and Chelsea detected unusual activity on 24 November 2025, invoked emergency arrangements, and confirmed that files were exfiltrated from IT infrastructure shared with Westminster City Council and the London Borough of Hammersmith and Fulham; the ICO was notified on 27 November and 22 December 2025 and the Metropolitan Police leads the investigation.
claims.exact_locator: S-005 paras 1.1, 4.1-4.3, 8.1; S-008 discovery and data sections
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Primary account of a shared-service attack on a public-sector project owner
claims.limitations: Data scope and personal-data volume not quantified

claims.claim_text: At Kensington and Chelsea, planning and licensing applications could not be processed normally until the planning and land-search system returned on 9 March 2026; repairs ran on backup systems with lower call volumes; core finance was constrained, with a controlled payment run processing over GBP 5 million of invoices; and revenues and benefits systems were unavailable from November 2025 to early June 2026.
claims.exact_locator: S-005 paras 5.4-5.8; S-006 paras 3.2-3.6; S-008 services section
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Shows owner-side outages reaching planning consent, repairs ordering and supplier payment, the processes contractors depend on
claims.limitations: No measure of contractor-side delay or loss is published

claims.claim_text: Kensington and Chelsea recorded GBP 1.2 million of cyber costs in 2025/26; its external auditor reported a significant governance weakness linked to the November 2025 incident, stated that the incident was caused by human error and that recovery was affected by the fragmented nature of the council's ICT estate, and listed further recovery costs as an unquantified risk.
claims.exact_locator: Minutes Item 5 p.8; AAR p.9 (agenda p.33); AAR pp.21, 23
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Only quantified public cost and assurance outcome among the in-period sector cases
claims.limitations: Covers 2025/26 only; insurance position not disclosed

claims.claim_text: Westminster stated that copied data sat in the shared environment hosted by Kensington and Chelsea and that it was working with the National Crime Agency, NCSC and the Metropolitan Police; Hammersmith and Fulham reported no evidence that its own systems were compromised.
claims.exact_locator: S-009 article body; S-005 para 4.1
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Shows partial containment across a three-authority shared service
claims.limitations: Statements relayed by specialist media

claims.claim_text: Sweden's data protection authority fined Miljödata SEK 1.8 million on 22 September 2026 under GDPR Article 32(1) after the August 2025 attack affecting about 2.2 million people, citing insufficient checks when installing new software and no automatic real-time intrusion monitoring, and opened investigations into two municipalities and one region; affected customers include a majority of Swedish municipalities (regulator) and, per secondary reporting, regions, state agencies and companies.
claims.exact_locator: S-010 decision notice; S-011 attack date 25 August 2025
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Demonstrates single-supplier concentration across public owners and companies and supervisory reach to customers
claims.limitations: Customer counts not stated by IMY; full decision not reviewed

claims.claim_text: Minnesota reported malicious activity at more than 30 community water systems on 26-27 July 2026, mostly involving remotely accessible PLCs and HMIs; the state stressed that impacted does not necessarily mean service disruption, made no attribution, and reported no requests to change drinking-water use.
claims.exact_locator: S-012 body; S-013 definition, attribution and recommended actions
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Malicious activity at public-works operational technology during the reporting period
claims.limitations: Operational effects still being assessed by the state

claims.claim_text: Media reporting citing unnamed officials described a preliminary assessment that Iran was likely responsible for the Minnesota activity; one affected town isolated its system, restored from backup and restarted its plant within about 90 minutes.
claims.exact_locator: S-014 article body; S-013 attribution status
alternative_hypotheses: Actors may be posing as Iran-based
claims.contrary_evidence: State officially made no attribution
claims.sector_relevance: Links public-works OT intrusion to the 2026 geopolitical context
claims.limitations: Anonymous, preliminary attribution

claims.claim_text: SANKO TECHNO, a Japanese supplier of post-installed anchors and fasteners for construction, disclosed on 28 August 2026 that ransomware had encrypted servers and PCs at its Vietnamese subsidiary, detected on 25 August; the subsidiary network was isolated, no group-wide impact was confirmed and the financial effect remained under review.
claims.exact_locator: S-015 disclosure body; S-016 business description
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: In-period building-materials supplier incident showing containment by network segregation
claims.limitations: No financial or delivery impact disclosed

claims.claim_text: Norway's Police Security Service confirmed on 13 August 2025 that it was investigating two connected attacks on Norwegian industrial systems including the Bremanger dam and described them as methods Russia uses to influence the security situation; QBE reports that outflow valves were opened for about four hours and that weak password protection and poor IT/OT separation were root causes.
claims.exact_locator: S-017 news body; S-018 Z-Pentest case study
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: European precedent of state-aligned manipulation of public-works OT
claims.limitations: Observation (April 2025) slightly outside the 18-month horizon; contextual only

claims.claim_text: The ICO fined construction and outsourcing group Interserve GBP 4.4 million after a phishing email led to malware, compromise of 283 systems and 16 accounts, removal of anti-virus and encryption of staff personal data; failings included not investigating an alert, outdated systems, inadequate training and insufficient risk assessment. QBE reports a further GBP 7 million of recovery and advisory fees.
claims.exact_locator: S-030 news body; S-018 costs section
claims.contrary_evidence: Staff-affected count differs between ICO article and video
claims.sector_relevance: Enduring construction precedent for regulatory and recovery cost after an identity-led intrusion
claims.limitations: Historical (2020 incident, 2022 penalty); recovery fee figure is secondary

claims.claim_text: On 28 September 2025 the UK Government backed a commercial bank loan of up to GBP 1.5 billion to Jaguar Land Rover through a UK Export Finance guarantee typically covering up to 80% of lender risk, repayable over five years, explicitly to support the supply chain during the cyber-related production shutdown.
claims.exact_locator: Release body and notes to editors
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Cross-sector precedent showing cyber disruption transmitting to supplier liquidity and bank lending
claims.limitations: Automotive case; not a construction event

claims.claim_text: Procore reported 17,850 customers running projects in about 160 countries at 31 December 2025 and states that it relies on third-party data centres such as AWS to host its platform, that customers depend on continuous availability and have a low tolerance for interruptions.
claims.exact_locator: Item 1; Item 1A risk factors on third-party data centres
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Evidence of shared construction-management SaaS with a hyperscale fourth party
claims.limitations: Customer count excludes some acquired customers; market share not disclosed

claims.claim_text: Construction had the highest number of company insolvencies in England and Wales in the 12 months to July 2026, with 3,841 cases or 17% of cases where industry was recorded.
claims.exact_locator: Industry breakdown paragraph
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Context for counterparty fragility when cyber shocks delay payment or schedule; a count, not a rate
claims.limitations: Not cyber-related; industry recorded for a subset of cases

claims.claim_text: NIS2 applies from 18 October 2024; its annexes cover sectors including drinking water, waste water, road transport authorities, public administration and specified manufacturing subsectors but do not list construction; Article 21(2)(d) requires supply-chain security measures, Article 23(4) sets 24-hour, 72-hour and one-month reporting steps, and Article 20 makes management bodies accountable for approving and overseeing measures.
claims.contrary_evidence: Member States may extend scope nationally
claims.sector_relevance: Construction firms mostly meet NIS2 through contracts with in-scope owners rather than direct designation
claims.limitations: National transposition and scope extensions vary

claims.claim_text: On 8 July 2026 the European Commission referred Ireland, Spain, France and the Netherlands to the Court of Justice for not notifying full NIS2 transposition and asked for lump-sum and daily penalties; letters of formal notice were sent on 28 November 2024 and reasoned opinions on 7 May 2025.
claims.exact_locator: News body
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Contractors operating across these markets face uneven national obligations
claims.limitations: National status may change after the referral

claims.claim_text: The CER Directive required transposition by 17 October 2024 and identification of designated entities by Member States by 17 July 2026; construction is not an Annex sector, but designated operators in transport, water and other sectors procure construction and maintenance work.
claims.exact_locator: Arts 6(1), 26(1); Annex
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: In-period milestone that can push resilience requirements into infrastructure construction contracts
claims.limitations: Contract flow-down is an inference, not a legal obligation on contractors

claims.claim_text: The Cyber Resilience Act entered into force on 10 December 2024; manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents from 11 September 2026 through ENISA's Single Reporting Platform (24-hour early warning, 72-hour notification, final report), with the main obligations applying from 11 December 2027.
claims.exact_locator: S-035 ELI metadata and Arts 14, 71; S-036 page body
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Reaches building-automation controllers, connected site equipment and construction software sold in the EU
claims.limitations: Applies to manufacturers of products with digital elements, not to contractors as users

claims.claim_text: GDPR Articles 28, 32 and 33 require processor contracts, appropriate security and notification to the supervisory authority within 72 hours where feasible; the UK Data Protection Act 2018 supplements the retained UK GDPR framework.
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Data exfiltration at contractors and owners triggers regulatory exposure independent of operational impact
claims.limitations: UK amendments after 2018 not reviewed

claims.claim_text: On 9 September 2026 the Commission proposed a Public Procurement Act regulation, COM(2026) 590, to replace the procurement directives; its explanatory memorandum describes provisions on cybersecurity compliance, security of supply and resilience, and exclusion of operators during contract performance for security reasons.
claims.exact_locator: Cover page; explanatory memorandum Chapter 4; recitals 29-30
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Signals future cyber and resilience conditions in EU public-works contracts
claims.limitations: Proposal only; subject to co-decision; article numbering not reviewed

claims.claim_text: The UK Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill, introduced in November 2025, remained in the House of Lords at report stage on 13 October 2026 (HL Bill 49 as amended in Grand Committee, 7 September 2026) and is not yet law.
claims.exact_locator: S-039 bill page; S-019 introduction month
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Main UK reform affecting managed service providers and designated suppliers to regulated operators
claims.limitations: Content and commencement may change

claims.claim_text: The UK NIS Regulations 2018 cover energy, transport, health, drinking water and digital infrastructure plus relevant digital service providers; construction is not an in-scope sector.
claims.exact_locator: Reg 1(1); Schedule 1; Schedule 2 para 7
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: UK construction exposure to NIS arises through operators of essential services as clients
claims.limitations: As-made text; amendments not reviewed

claims.claim_text: PPN 014 requires central government in-scope bodies, from 24 February 2025, to require Cyber Essentials or equivalent controls for higher-risk contracts and leaves application optional for other public bodies; the Procurement Act 2023 regime also went live on 24 February 2025.
claims.exact_locator: S-040 scope, requirement, paras 6 and 10; S-042 briefing body
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Sets the contractual cyber baseline for suppliers to UK central government projects
claims.limitations: Local authorities not mandated; Cyber Essentials is a baseline, not resilience assurance

claims.claim_text: ISO 19650-5:2020 sets a security-minded approach to information management for built assets and BIM and was confirmed after systematic review in October 2025; NIST CSF 2.0 (February 2024) is a voluntary outcomes framework including supply-chain risk management; the SEC requires US registrants to file Form 8-K Item 1.05 within four business days of determining that an incident is material.
claims.exact_locator: S-043 abstract and status; S-044 publication page; S-047 guide
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Voluntary frameworks give a control vocabulary; SEC rules shape disclosure by US-listed sector participants
claims.limitations: Standards are voluntary and not binding law; SEC rule is comparative only

claims.claim_text: Principal judgement 1: the best-documented Building & Public Works propagation pathway in the period runs through shared digital layers - owner shared services, sector SaaS and cloud hosting - because the best-documented in-period disruptions (Kensington and Chelsea, Miljödata) propagated across many dependent organisations; leak-site data show many more construction ransomware claims than public disclosures.
claims.exact_locator: See C-013 to C-017 and C-024
alternative_hypotheses: Leak-site data show many more construction ransomware claims than public disclosures, so direct attacks may dominate
claims.contrary_evidence: Leak-site data (Dragos, Black Kite) show many direct contractor attacks
claims.sector_relevance: Directs management attention to concentration and propagation, the channels with systemic reach
claims.limitations: Public evidence is skewed to public bodies that must report; private contractor disruptions are under-disclosed

claims.claim_text: Principal judgement 2: in construction, IT disruption converts into schedule loss quickly where work depends on time-sensitive, sequenced operations such as marine placement, tunnelling or site access, so the cost driver is programme delay and contractual allocation rather than IT recovery alone.
claims.exact_locator: QBE delay and cost statements; Femern reported effects
alternative_hypotheses: Contract buffers and float may absorb short outages
claims.contrary_evidence: No in-period contractor has disclosed a quantified cyber-driven delay
claims.sector_relevance: Explains why cyber events can escalate into project cost overrun and counterparty stress
claims.limitations: Femern effects unconfirmed; QBE quantification partly undisclosed

claims.claim_text: Principal judgement 3: internet-exposed public-works OT is an active pressure point - a national authority warned of opportunistic Iranian targeting and unattributed malicious activity followed at Minnesota water systems - with construction firms more likely to be collateral or access-path victims than primary targets; no baseline shows a rise.
alternative_hypotheses: Activity may be opportunistic or criminal scanning rather than state direction
claims.contrary_evidence: State attribution for Minnesota not made
claims.sector_relevance: Translates threat-actor intent into geopolitical exposure for public-works owners and their contractors
claims.limitations: Attribution is preliminary or contextual

claims.claim_text: Principal judgement 4: financial-system transmission is conditional and runs through contractor working capital, owner payment delays, supplier insolvency, guarantees and emergency lending rather than direct bank loss; the sector's leading insolvency count is context (a count, not a rate).
alternative_hypotheses: Large contractors may absorb shocks through liquidity buffers
claims.contrary_evidence: No in-period case showed a contractor default linked to cyber
claims.sector_relevance: Explains generic bank relevance without asserting any bank's exposure
claims.limitations: Channels inferred from analogous and partial evidence

claims.claim_text: Principal judgement 5: the regulatory perimeter for construction is mostly indirect - construction is not an NIS2, CER or UK NIS sector - so obligations arrive through owners' supply-chain duties, procurement conditions, product rules under the CRA and data-protection law, with uneven national NIS2 application.
alternative_hypotheses: Some Member States may extend NIS2 to construction-related entities
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Indicates where compliance pressure and contract change will reach contractors
claims.limitations: National extensions not surveyed exhaustively

claims.claim_text: Case selection: Kensington and Chelsea was selected over the Femern contractor incident because it combines Tier 1 chronology, disclosed cost, auditor findings and service-level restoration dates, whereas the Femern evidence is one to two days old and discloses no cause, duration or cost.
claims.exact_locator: Selection matrix in report Chapter 5
alternative_hypotheses: Femern has higher subsector relevance and may supersede in the next edition
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Prioritises causal clarity and disclosed outcomes for a standalone lesson
claims.limitations: Council is a project owner, not a contractor

claims.claim_text: Public financial disclosure gap: none of the in-period contractor or supplier incidents reviewed disclosed a quantified cost, contractual effect or project delay; quantified outcomes come from a public body (GBP 1.2 million) and regulators (SEK 1.8 million; historical GBP 4.4 million).
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Prevents false precision in loss estimates and supports scenario-based analysis
claims.limitations: Absence of disclosure is not evidence of no loss

claims.claim_text: Case lessons: a shared IT estate with fragmented legacy systems, a human-error entry point and multi-month restoration of revenue, planning and finance functions are transferable risks for public owners and for contractors that depend on owner approvals and payments.
alternative_hypotheses: Council-specific legacy systems may limit transferability
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Gives a recovery benchmark (about 15 weeks for planning, about six months for revenues) for owner-dependency planning
claims.limitations: Root-cause review not yet published

claims.claim_text: Scenario 1 assumption: a multi-day availability failure (without data compromise) of a widely used construction-management or common-data-environment platform, or of its hosting cloud region, removes access to drawings, RFIs, permits-to-work and payment applications for many contractors and owners at once.
alternative_hypotheses: Offline copies and alternative channels may limit impact
claims.contrary_evidence: No in-period sector-wide platform outage was identified
claims.sector_relevance: Tests common digital-dependency concentration
claims.limitations: Structured stress narrative, not a forecast

claims.claim_text: Scenario 2 assumption: ransomware or OT intrusion at a major contractor or public-works operator halts time-sensitive site, marine or plant operations during a sequenced programme phase for one to four weeks.
alternative_hypotheses: Manual workarounds may sustain safety-relevant operations
claims.contrary_evidence: Minnesota town restored within about 90 minutes
claims.sector_relevance: Tests targeted operational disruption
claims.limitations: Duration band derived from the QBE 24-day average and is illustrative

claims.claim_text: Scenario 3 assumption: a compromise spreading through a shared supplier's access, data or payment relationships - a public-sector software supplier, managed service provider or building-materials manufacturer - simultaneously disrupts multiple owners, contractors and programmes and triggers data-protection duties across its customers.
alternative_hypotheses: Supplier diversity may limit simultaneous effects
claims.contrary_evidence: SANKO TECHNO contained impact to one subsidiary
claims.sector_relevance: Tests third- and fourth-party concentration
claims.limitations: Structured stress narrative, not a forecast

claims.claim_text: Mitigation priority: the evidence supports prioritising owner and platform dependency mapping, identity and remote-access hardening, OT and site-system segregation, payment-change verification, contractual cyber clauses with flow-down, and tested manual fallback for programme-time-sensitive operations.
claims.exact_locator: Chapter 7 action table
alternative_hypotheses: Priorities may differ for SMEs versus tier-1 contractors
claims.contrary_evidence: None identified in the reviewed source set
claims.sector_relevance: Links each action to an evidenced exposure for 1LoD challenge
claims.limitations: Sector priorities, not an assessment of any bank or firm
